\title{Sparse Attention for Long Documents}

\begin{abstract}
We study attention patterns that reduce the quadratic cost of self-attention on long inputs, and report accuracy and speed on three benchmarks.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Transformers scale poorly with sequence length~\citep{vaswani2017}. Several sparse patterns have been proposed~\citep{child2019,beltagy2020}. We make three contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item a block-sparse pattern with $O(n\sqrt{n})$ cost;
  \item a training recipe that keeps accuracy within 1\% of dense attention;
  \item an open implementation at \url{https://example.org/sparse}.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
Let $Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ be the queries, keys and values. The dense output is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dense}
  \mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V.
\end{equation}
Our block pattern restricts the score matrix to blocks of size $b$, as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:dense} with a mask $M$.
\begin{align}
  \mathcal{C}_{\text{dense}} &= O(n^2 d) \label{eq:cost-dense} \\
  \mathcal{C}_{\text{ours}} &= O(n\sqrt{n}\,d) \label{eq:cost-ours}
\end{align}

    Dense & 81.2 & 77.4 & 69.0 \\
    Ours & 80.9 & 77.1 & 68.6 \\

Results are in Table~\ref{tab:acc}; the cost trade-off is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:pattern}. As Eq.~\eqref{eq:cost-ours} shows, the savings grow with $n$.

\section{Conclusion}
Sparse blocks give most of the accuracy at a fraction of the cost.
